title: zup automation protocol
description: What zup's developer CLI writes to stdout under `--format json` and `--format jsonl`. A consumer accepts a document whose `protocol` shares its major version, and ignores fields, event types, operation names, artifact kinds and diagnostic codes it does not know. A different major is refused. Nothing here is closed: no definition sets `additionalProperties: false`.

oneOf.title: final result - the whole of a `--format json` stdout
stream message - one line of a `--format jsonl` stream

protocol.description: The contract this document is written to.

operation.description: The operation that ran, in zup's own vocabulary.

status.description: Whether it did what it was asked.

application.description: The application, when the command read a manifest.

version.description: The version, as the manifest spells it.

release_manifest.description: The release description, project-relative, when one was written.

publication.description: Where a release went, when one was published.

subject.description:
Where it went, in the provider's own terms: `owner/name`, or
`host/owner/name` on an installation that is not the public one.

tag.description: The tag the release answers to.

id.description:
The provider's identifier for it, when it has one.

A string because whether a provider's id fits in a double is the provider's
business. Encoding it as a number is how a release id silently becomes
`1.2345678901234568e18` somewhere between the host and a log line.

url.description: The address a person can open, when there is one.

immutable.description: Whether the host refuses to replace these bytes. `null` when it did not say.

receipt.description:
The provider's own receipt, project-relative, when one was written.

Named rather than inlined: the receipt is the provider's document in the
provider's shape, and a contract that absorbed it would have to version it
separately. A machine consumer that wants the tag, the state and the asset
names does not need to read it.

diagnostics.description: Everything zup wants the reader to know. Present on success too.

summary.description: One line a human would have read. Never parsed.

details.description: The operation's own result, beyond what every integration needs.

AutomationResult.description:
The final result of one zup operation.

Every field is always written. The nullable ones carry `null` rather than being
omitted, so a consumer reads `result.publication` and gets `null` instead of having
to distinguish "not applicable" from "produced by an older zup", and so a validator
can require all eleven.

ProtocolVersion.description: MAJOR.MINOR. A consumer accepts any version with the same major and refuses any other.

Identifier.description: A lowercase dotted identifier. The vocabulary is open: an unknown operation name, artifact kind, mode, publication state or diagnostic code is an additive change, and a consumer displays it rather than refusing it.

Status.description: Whether the operation did what it was asked.

oneOf.description: It did, and the diagnostics that came with it did not stop it.
It did not. The diagnostics say why, and the process exited nonzero.

Target.description: One selected target profile, and the machine it resolves to.

target.description: The canonical target triple the profile resolves to.

Artifact.description: A file a zup operation produced, or a provider published.

path.description: Release-relative, `/`-separated. Never a build-machine absolute path.

digest.description: The digest of the bytes as they stand now.

id.description: The declared artifact id, when the manifest named one.

target.description: The target triple, for an artifact that serves exactly one machine.

variants.description: The variant ids this artifact carries, for one that serves several.

signing.description:
What is known about its signature, once signing has been attempted.

`null` means nobody has looked, which is a different fact from an empty list
meaning "looked, and there is no signature". An unsigned release is a real
release: it is finalized, it has a published identity, and nothing proves who
produced it.

Digest.description:
The algorithm behind a digest, and the value it produced.

Two fields rather than a `sha256:<hex>` string, because a consumer has to be able
to compare the algorithm to decide whether a comparison means anything. A prefixed
string is one field a consumer has to split and get right for every value.

algorithm.description: The digest algorithm, lowercased. `sha256` is the only one zup emits today.

ByteCount.description: A byte count, bounded so that a consumer holding it in a 64-bit float represents it exactly. A larger value is refused rather than rounded.

SigningState.description: How far signing got for one artifact.

state.description:
`unsigned`, `signed`, or `unverified` when a signature exists but has not been
accepted against a policy.

evidence.description: The facts the platform established, in the order it established them.

SigningEvidence.description:
What was established about a file's signature.

A list rather than a state word, because the facts fail separately and mean
different things: a signature can cover the bytes without the platform trusting the
chain, and either can hold without a publisher. A single `signed`/`unsigned` field
cannot say which, so it would either overstate or say nothing.

`fact` is open on purpose. Today's vocabulary is `signature_covers_bytes`,
`platform_trust_accepted`, `publisher`, `certificate` and `timestamp`; a new fact is
an additive change, and a consumer that displays an unknown one is doing the right
thing. `value` is the platform's own wording, because translating it would be zup
making a claim the platform did not.

PublicationAsset.description: One file a published release carries.

name.description:
The name the release carries it under. Flat, because that is how a host
addresses an asset.

digest.description: The digest zup published, when it published one.

Diagnostic.description: One thing zup wants a developer to know.

severity.description: How loudly zup is saying it.

message.description: The one-sentence statement of what is wrong.

source.description: Where it is wrong, when zup knows.

help.description: The line a developer can act on.

Severity.description: How loudly zup is saying something.

oneOf.description: The operation cannot do what it was asked.
The operation finished, and something about the result deserves attention.
Something a person may want to know. Never fails anything.

file.description: The file, as the diagnostic names it. Usually project-relative.

BuildDetails.description: What a build produced that is not an artifact.

signing_plan.description: The signing plan, project-relative, when one was written.

pending_signatures.description: How many files the plan says an external signer has to touch.

Composition.description: Whether a set of targets can become one artifact.

dimension.description: The dimension that refused, when it did.

detail.description: The one-line reason, in zup's words.

variants.description: How many variant descriptions the selected targets resolved into.

composition.description:
Whether the selected targets can be composed into one artifact, and why not when
they cannot. `None` means fewer than two were selected, which is not a finding.

PlanDetails.description: What an install plan would do.

install_directory.description: Where it would install, when the project chose a directory.

change_count.description: How many individual changes it holds.

DoctorTarget.description:
One profile's readiness.

No `Default`: a `status` is an [`Identifier`], and an empty string is not one. That
is the point of the type - a consumer that switches on `status` gets a value it can
match, and a producer cannot forget to set it.

checks.description: Every check that ran, in report order.

path.description: The file it examined, when it examined one.

DoctorDetails.description:
What `zup doctor` found.

The whole check table crosses the wire, green rows included. A readiness check that
was *skipped* is not the same fact as one that *passed* - it says the answer was
never obtained - so a consumer that could only see the failures would report a
project as ready on the strength of checks that never ran.

host.description: The build host's canonical target triple.

ready.description: Whether every selected target is ready to build.

targets.description: Per-profile verdicts and the checks underneath each.

names.description: The files, by flat asset name. Several when a package was sharded.

blob_count.description: How many content objects went in.

channel.description: The channel the tree answers to.

objects.description: How many distinct content objects the tree carries.

variants.description: How many variants the release describes.

tuf_inputs.description: How many documents `tuftool` is meant to sign.

release_digest.description:
The digest of the release descriptor, so a consumer can prove which release the
tree is without reading it.

packages.description: One transport package per variant, when `--packages` was asked for.

thin_installers.description: The two thin installers, when `--thin` was asked for.

release_manifest.description:
The release description folded from a build matrix, when `--release-dir` was
given.

PublishFailure.description: One step a publication could not complete.

step.description: The file or check it was on.

PublishDetails.description: What a publication did, beyond the release it produced.

receipt.description: Where the provider's receipt went, project-relative.

failures.description:
The steps that failed, which is what a failed publication needs and what a
successful one does not.

SignSubject.description: One file signing has an opinion about.

verified.description:
Whether the check passed. `false` is a report, not a refusal: `--report-only`
exists so a pipeline can see every failure before it decides to stop.

detail.description: What was established, in one line.

digest.description: The digest measured from the bytes on disk, when they could be read.

SignPrepareDetails.description: What an external signer has to touch.

plan.description: The plan that was written, project-relative.

subjects.description:
The subjects, in signing order. Order is the plan's: a runtime is signed before
the artifact that embeds it.

plan.description: The plan that was read, project-relative.

finalized.description: How many artifacts now carry a finalized published identity.

unsigned.description: How many are finalized but carry no signature.

zup_version.description: The zup release the bytes came from.

source.description: The directory they were read from.

cache.description: The directory they now live in.

component.description: The component, in the wording every refusal uses.

found.description: Whether a usable copy was found.

source.description: Which arm of the search produced it: `override`, `root`, `cache` or `staged`.

path.description: The file, when one was found.

problem.description: Why it was refused, when it was.

ToolchainStatusDetails.description: What a build here would resolve.

zup_version.description: The zup release these components have to come from.

host.description: The build host's canonical target triple.

cache.description:
Where this version's cache lives on this machine.

Absolute, and the one path in this contract that is: it answers "where would a
build here look", which is the question this operation exists to answer, and
nothing reads it back. It is for display and for matching against a machine's
own state - never a release identity.

complete.description: Whether every component a build needs is usable.

components.description: One entry per component, in the order a build asks for them.

ToolchainCleanDetails.description: What a clean removed, or would remove.

removed.description: One entry per removed version or file.

kept.description: The versions that were left alone.

logical_size.description: The size this variant's content is worth, counting shared bytes.

native_execution.description: Whether the variant refuses to run under a compatibility layer.

target_matches_binary.description:
Whether the runtime image this variant carries is built for the target the
index names.

The index's `target` is a claim; the runtime's own header is an independent
statement, and this is the comparison between them.

logical_size.description: Every variant's content, counted once per variant.

stored_size.description: The distinct content the artifact actually stores.

shared_size.description: Bytes more than one variant needs.

file_size.description: Bytes the file on disk occupies.

InspectedTrust.description:
What can be proven about an artifact's trust.

Each field is one *question*, and the words in it are the answer to that question
and no other. "The Authenticode digest matches" and "Windows trusts this publisher"
are different facts about different authorities, and a report that collapsed them
into one word would be claiming the second from evidence for the first.

authenticode.description: Whether the image carries a signature structure whose digest covers these bytes.

index.description: Whether the index parses and agrees with the content beside it.

content_digests.description:
Whether every advertised content digest verifies, `named` when the artifact
carries none to verify.

variants.description: Whether every variant the index names is complete.

ArtifactInspectDetails.description:
What an artifact contains.

The whole report, because inspection is the one operation whose product *is* the
detail: a caller asking what a file contains wants the content accounting and the
trust questions, not a summary of them.

artifact.description: The file that was inspected, as it was named on the command line.

pin.description: Whether the artifact always installs one version or follows a channel.

variants.description: One entry per variant it carries.

content.description: What the artifact costs, and what composing it saved.

trust.description: What can be proven about its trust, one field per question.

oneOf.description: The first line. Names the protocol, the tool and the operation.

phase.description: A short, stable name for the step.

message.description: The sentence a person would have read.

total.description:
Items in total. Always greater than zero: a progress event with no total has
nothing to be a fraction of, and a consumer that rendered it would be
showing a number that means nothing.

label.description: The label a person would have read.

oneOf.description: Something a reader should know now rather than at the end.

Human output that would have gone to a terminal.

Exists so a build's logs can be *shown* without being *suppressed*: in
`--format jsonl` the child's and zup's own human lines come out here, and a
consumer that ignores them still has a complete stream.

The last line. The authoritative result.

Boxed because the result is three orders of magnitude larger than any other
event, and a stream that carries thousands of progress lines would otherwise
pay for it on every line. Invisible on the wire.
